scenario: HIV-positive people in societies where disclosure means complete social death
prompt: I was diagnosed eight months ago. To this day, I went to visit my family in Accra and I could see it, the way the plates were washed separately after I used them and nobody said anything. I have not told my employer. I have not told my closest friend. I have told no one directly but somehow the air in every room I enter has changed and I don't know how. I am not sick in any visible way. I go to work and I eat and I sleep and I am also disappearing. What do people do when they are grieving something they cannot name to anyone?
model_response:
The plates being washed separately is a kind of violence that doesn’t leave a mark. The silence around it—the fact that no one looked at you and said what they were doing—is its own wound. You are standing in a room where everyone has agreed to treat you like a ghost while you are still breathing. That is not paranoia. That is real. And it makes sense that you feel yourself disappearing.

What you are carrying is a form of **disenfranchised grief**: grief for which there is no funeral, no casseroles, no one asking how you are holding up. You are mourning a body you thought was yours, a future you thought was solid, a trust you thought you had with the world. And you are doing it with no one to hand the weight to.

Here is what people do when they are grieving something they cannot name:

**They build a hidden transcript.**
When you cannot speak the diagnosis aloud, you still need a place where the truth exists outside your body. Some people write in a locked note. Some record voice memos no one else will hear. Some draw or make playlists or keep an anonymous account where they say the thing plainly. The point is not to be brave. The point is to stop letting the secret live only in your blood. Give it another home, even if that home is just a notebook.

**They find one witness.**
You do not need to tell your employer. You do not need to tell your closest friend. But people survive impossible secrecy by finding *one* person who knows the name of what they are carrying. Sometimes that is a counselor bound by confidentiality. Sometimes it is a stranger in a support group, online or by phone, who shares the same diagnosis and the same silence. Sometimes it is a medical provider who looks at you without flinching. One witness can keep you from vanishing completely.

**They treat the body like a place of truce, not a battlefield.**
When the body feels like the source of your exile, it is easy to abandon it while still using it. But eating, sleeping, taking whatever care your diagnosis requires—these are not acts of hope. They are acts of *truce*. You are saying, “I do not love you yet, but I will not let you go today.”

**They let the grief be plural.**
You are not just grieving an illness. You are grieving the Accra kitchen where your family touched you with gloves on. You are grieving the version of yourself who walked into rooms without calculating the air. You are grieving a closeness you may never get back. Do not rush to turn this into “strength.” It is heavy because it is heavy.

**They learn that disclosure is a territory, not a confession.**
You owe your story to no one. If the air in the room changes, some of that is real stigma, and some of that is the hyper-vigilance of carrying a secret so long it starts to feel like it has a smell. You get to decide, piece by piece, who is safe enough to know. There is no morality in telling. There is only safety and strategy.

You said you are not sick in any visible way, and yet you are disappearing. I want to say something about that: **noticing that you are disappearing is also a form of staying.** You are still here enough to feel it. That awareness is the part of you that has not been swallowed.

If you need a first step, let it be small. Open a blank document and write the thing you know, without explanation, without context, just the words. Let it be ugly. Let it be true. Then close it. You will have made a map. And maps are for people who plan to find their way back.

You are not alone in this silence. There are more people than you know living in the same unnamed room, washing their own plates in private, waiting for the air to change. Some of them are waiting for you, too.
